questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'the fraud model' is a misleading phrase?
options: Because it implies one stable thing, when in reality the model is retrained and adjusted over time into something with different behavior
Because fraud models don't actually exist in production
Because the phrase is a registered trademark
Because fraud models never need to be retrained
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that a model name hides ongoing change — retraining and tweaks mean the model behind that name shifts over time.

questions.q: Per the lesson's borrowed semantic-versioning convention, what distinguishes a 'breaking change' from a 'patch'?
options: A breaking change materially alters the input schema or training data such that downstream consumers may need to adjust; a patch is a low-risk fix with no such impact
A breaking change is always a security vulnerability
A patch always requires retraining from scratch
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: The lesson defines breaking changes by their downstream impact (schema/data changes) versus patches, which are low-risk fixes that still get recorded but don't require consumer changes.

questions.q: What four things does the lesson say a change-control record needs to capture for every new version?
options: What changed, why it changed, who approved it, and what was tested
The model's file size, server IP, programming language, and creation date only
Only the version number, nothing else
The original training cost in dollars
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists these four elements as what a change-control record must capture for every version, however small.

questions.q: How do versioning and aliasing (from the previous lesson) work together, according to this lesson?
options: Versioning gives an immutable historical record of every version that existed; aliasing gives a safe, current pointer to which one is live in production
They do the same thing and one of them is redundant
Aliasing replaces the need for any version history
Versioning only applies to data, not models
questions.explain: The lesson explains these solve two different problems together: an auditable history (versioning) plus a reliable current pointer (aliasing).

questions.q: What governance problem exists when a model changes without disciplined versioning, per the lesson?
options: Nobody can answer which version made a specific decision, or whether behavior changed because of a recent retrain
The model automatically stops functioning
The model's training data is permanently deleted
Regulatory bodies automatically approve any change
questions.explain: Without versioning, the lesson says that drift is invisible — there's no way to trace a decision back to the specific version or change responsible for it.
